n01.q: In “She looks ____ today”, which word is correct?
n01.e: Look is a linking verb, so it is followed by an adjective that describes the subject: She looks happy. Happily is an adverb and cannot follow a linking verb.

n01.q: What part of speech is “fast” in “He drives fast”?
n01.e: Fast describes how he drives, so it is an adverb here. Fast has the same form as an adjective and an adverb.

n01.q: What part of speech is “drink” in “I need a drink”?
n01.e: After the article a, the word is a noun. The same word, drink, is a verb in We drink tea.

n01.q: Which sentence uses the pattern S + V + O + O?
n01.e: Gave has two objects: me (indirect object) and a book (direct object), so the pattern is S + V + O + O.

n01.q: Which word is a linking verb?
n01.e: Seem links the subject to a complement (He seems tired). Run, write and carry are action verbs.
Taste is a linking verb here, so an adjective (delicious) follows. Adverbs such as deliciously describe actions, not the subject's quality.

n01.q: In “Wow! That was amazing!”, “Wow” is a(n) ____.
n01.e: An interjection expresses sudden feeling and stands apart from the sentence grammar, like Wow!, Oh! and Oops!

n01.q: In “She bought those books”, which word is a determiner?
n01.e: Those comes before the noun books and shows which ones: it is a determiner. Books is a noun, bought is a verb and She is a pronoun.

n01.q: In “The teacher praised him”, which word is a pronoun?
n01.e: Him is the object form of a pronoun: it replaces the noun phrase the teacher praised. Pronouns replace nouns.

n01.q: Which sentence has the pattern S + V + C?
n01.e: Became is a linking verb, so the pattern is S + V + C: tired describes the students. In the other sentences the verbs take an object or no complement.

n01.q: In “The book is on the table”, the word “on” is a(n) ____.
n01.e: On shows where the book is in relation to the table, so it is a preposition. A conjunction would join two clauses.
Well is the adverb that describes the verb speaks. Good is an adjective and cannot describe a verb; an adverb cannot be placed between the verb and its object.

n02.e: A consonant + y changes to -ies in the plural: city becomes cities. Vowel + y only adds -s (days).
Drop the silent -e before -ing: make becomes making. The only exceptions are words like be (being) and see (seeing).
Stop is a short word that ends in one vowel + one consonant, so the final consonant doubles before -ed: stopped.
Its (no apostrophe) shows possession, like his or her. It's is only short for it is or it has.

o: Sokha, my friend, lives in Takeo.
Sokha my friend, lives in Takeo.
Sokha, my friend lives in Takeo.
Sokha my friend lives, in Takeo.
n02.e: The commas go around extra information (my friend) that could be removed without changing the main sentence.
The rule is i before e, except after c: receive. Exceptions such as weird and science are words to learn separately.
Nouns ending in consonant + o often add -es: potatoes. A few, such as photos and pianos, only add -s.
The names of languages and nationalities always begin with a capital letter: Khmer. Student, teacher and class are common nouns.
Knife ends in -fe, which changes to -ves in the plural: knives. Many nouns with f or fe follow this rule (leaf, life, wolf).
A consonant + y changes to -ied in the past: study becomes studied. After a vowel, y stays (played).

n02.q: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
o: The teacher's pen is on the desk.
n02.e: An apostrophe + s shows possession for one owner (the teacher's pen). Do not use an apostrophe for plurals (apples) or in its, whose possessive has no apostrophe.

n02.q: Choose the correct punctuation: Where do you live ____
n02.e: A direct question ends with a question mark. A full stop is for statements and an exclamation mark for strong feeling.

n03.q: The ____ of the new school was a great success. (complete)
n03.e: After the, a noun is needed, so complete (adjective) becomes the noun completion. -tion is a common noun suffix.
Before a noun (student), an adjective is needed: successful. Success is a noun and successfully is an adverb.
The prefix im- is used before p, so the opposite of possible is impossible (and un-, in- do not fit).
An adverb describes a verb (answered), so careful becomes carefully by adding -ly.
The suffix -ness forms nouns from adjectives: kind becomes kindness. Kindly is an adverb and unkind is an adjective.
The prefix il- is used before l, so the opposite of legal is illegal.
A compound adjective before a noun uses a singular unit: a five-year-old child. Plural forms are used only when the phrase stands alone (She is five years old).

n03.q: We should ____ the rules to make them easier. (simple)
n03.e: The suffix -ify makes a verb from an adjective: simple becomes simplify, meaning to make simple.
The sentence needs a noun that names the quality: Her kindness helped me. Kindly is an adverb and kinder is a comparative adjective.
Irregular needs ir- before r, so the opposite of regular is irregular. Un-, in- and dis- do not fit this word.
A word is needed that can describe medicine and is formed from danger with -ous: dangerous. Dangerously is an adverb.
The prefix re- means again: rewrite is write again. Mis- means wrongly, pre- means before, and un- means not.

n04.q: She has ____ a letter to her friend.
n04.e: The Present Perfect needs the past participle (V3): has written. Wrote is V2 and cannot follow has.
The sentence is in the past simple, so use V2: drank. Drunk is V3 and needs have or has before it.

n04.q: The thief was ____ by the police.
n04.e: The passive needs be + V3: was caught. Catch – caught – caught.
Rise has no object and the verb after has needs V3: has risen. Rose is V2 and raised needs an object.

n04.q: The window was ____ by the ball.
n04.e: The passive needs was + V3: broken. Break – broke – broken.

n04.q: I ____ the book on the table yesterday.
n04.e: Lay (put) needs an object and its past is laid: I laid the book. Lay is also the past of lie, which is a different verb.

n04.q: Which verb has the same form in V1, V2 and V3?
n04.e: Cut has the same form in V1, V2 and V3. Bring, take and give all change.
The Present Perfect needs V3: have built. Build – built – built.
Ring – rang – rung: the Present Perfect needs V3, so has rung. Rang is the past simple.
Swim – swam – swum: has swum. Swam is V2 and cannot follow has.

n04.q: The ball was ____ over the wall.
n04.e: The passive needs be + V3: was thrown. Throw – threw – thrown.

o: She hanged the picture on the wall.
She has hunged the picture on the wall.
She hang the picture on the wall.
She hung the picture on the wall.
n04.e: Hang – hung – hung is used for objects like pictures. Hanged is only used for executions, and the other forms are not English.

n05.q: Look at the black clouds! It ____ rain.
n05.e: The speaker predicts the future from evidence they can see now (black clouds), so use be going to: is going to rain.
A decision made at the moment of speaking (the phone is ringing now) uses will: I'll answer it.

n05.q: I ____ Dara at five o'clock tomorrow. We have already arranged it.
n05.e: Already arranged plans with a time use the Present Continuous: I am meeting Dara at five.
Timetables and schedules use the Present Simple: The train leaves at 6.30.

n05.q: I will phone you when I ____ home.
n05.e: After when, use a present tense for the future, not will: I will phone you when I get home.

n05.q: If it ____ tomorrow, we will stay at home.
n05.e: After if, use the Present Simple for the future, not will: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
Be about to means the very near future: The film is about to start. It is used when something is going to happen immediately.
A plan decided before speaking uses be going to: I am going to study medicine.

n05.q: What time ____ the film start tonight? (cinema timetable)
n05.e: A cinema timetable uses the Present Simple, and the question needs do-support: What time does the film start?

n05.q: As soon as she ____ the exam results, she will call us.
n05.e: After as soon as, use a present tense for the future: As soon as she gets the results, she will call us.
A prediction based on opinion (I think) uses will: I think the exam will be difficult.
A warning from present evidence uses be going to: You are going to fall. The other options are not correct English.

n06.q: When I was a child, I ____ in Kampot.
n06.e: Used to + V1 describes a past state that is no longer true. Live is a state verb, so would is not used.
Be used to is followed by -ing or a noun: She is used to getting up early. To is a preposition here.

n06.q: Every summer we ____ to our grandparents' village.
n06.e: Would + V1 describes repeated past actions with a time frame (every summer). It is used for actions, not states.

n06.q: Did you ____ play football when you were young?
n06.e: After did, the form is use to, without -d: Did you use to play football?

n06.q: It took me a while to get used to ____ the heat.
n06.e: Get used to is followed by -ing or a noun: getting used to living in the heat. To is a preposition here.

n06.q: Which sentence is correct for a past state?
o: I would have long hair when I was young.
I used to have long hair.
I am used to have long hair.
I use to have long hair now.
n06.e: Have is a state verb, so used to is needed. Would is not used for past states, and the other options mix the structures.

n06.q: I ____ in Phnom Penh for five years.
n06.e: A period of stated length (five years) uses the Past Simple, not used to: I lived in Phnom Penh for five years.

n06.q: He ____ smoke, but he stopped last year.
n06.e: Used to + V1 describes a past habit that has ended: He used to smoke, but he stopped last year.

n06.q: When I was young, I didn't ____ like vegetables.
n06.e: After did not (didn't), use use to without -d: I didn't use to like vegetables.

n06.q: He has lived in Japan for years, so he is used to ____ chopsticks.
n06.e: Be used to is followed by -ing: He is used to using chopsticks. Used to and use cannot follow be.

o: I used to live in Takeo when I was a child.
Every Sunday we would visit my aunt.
I would live in Takeo when I was a child.
I am used to living in Takeo.
n06.e: Would is used for repeated actions, not for states: live is a state, so I used to live is correct. The other three sentences are all correct.

n06.q: It's hard to ____ living alone at first.
n06.e: After get used to, an -ing form follows: It's hard to get used to living alone. Used to + V1 describes past habits only.

n07.e: Know is a stative verb (a mental state), so it is not used in continuous tenses: I know the answer.
The situation is still true now (you live here now), so use the Present Perfect: How long have you lived here?
Yesterday is a finished time, so use the Past Simple: I lost my keys yesterday.

n07.q: She ____ emails all morning, so she is tired.
n07.e: All morning shows a continuing activity with a visible result (she is tired): Present Perfect Continuous.
A number of completed things (five letters) uses the Present Perfect Simple. The Continuous stresses the activity, not the result.

n07.q: When I arrived, the class ____ already ____.
n07.e: The class started before I arrived, so the earlier action uses the Past Perfect: had already started.

n07.q: He ____ a shower when the phone rang.
n07.e: Have in the sense of take (a shower) is an action, so it can be continuous: was having a shower. The phone ringing interrupted it.

o: I am having lunch with my friend.
n07.e: Have meaning eat is an action and can be continuous. Have meaning own, know and like are stative and are not used in the continuous.

n07.q: Sokha ____ TV when the lights went out.
n07.e: A longer action was in progress when the lights went out: Past Continuous, was watching.
Since 2022 needs the Present Perfect. Have meaning own is stative, so use have had, not have been having.

n07.q: I'm busy now. I ____ for my exam.
n07.e: Now shows an action in progress, so use the Present Continuous: I am studying for my exam.
Taste is used in the Present Simple when it describes a quality, not an action: This soup tastes delicious.

n08.q: You ____ park here. It is forbidden.
n08.e: Mustn't expresses prohibition (it is forbidden). Don't have to means that something is not necessary.

n08.q: You ____ come tomorrow. It's a holiday.
n08.e: Don't have to means not necessary: it's a holiday, so you are free. Mustn't would mean it is forbidden.

n08.q: She isn't answering. She ____ be asleep.
n08.e: Might expresses possibility: She might be asleep. Must would mean that you are almost sure.

n08.q: He ____ have left already. His coat has gone.
n08.e: His coat has gone is evidence, so the deduction is strong: must have + V3. Can't would mean it is impossible.

n08.q: The answer is wrong. It ____ be correct.
n08.e: The answer is wrong, so it is impossible that it is correct: can't. Must and should do not express impossibility.

n08.q: You ____ have told me earlier. Now it is too late.
n08.e: Should have + V3 expresses past criticism or regret: You should have told me earlier.

n08.q: I ____ finish the test in time. It was hard but I did it.
n08.e: Was able to is used for a specific past success (one occasion). Could is used for general ability in the past.

n08.q: You ____ better hurry or you'll miss the bus.
n08.e: Had better + V1 gives strong advice or a warning: You had better hurry. Should to and would to do not exist.

n08.q: I ____ rather stay at home tonight.
n08.e: Would rather + V1 expresses preference: I would rather stay home. Modals are not followed by to.
A modal is followed by the base verb with no to and no -s: She can swim.
May is a polite, formal way to ask for permission. Must, should and need do not ask for permission.

n08.q: Students ____ use phones in the exam. It is against the rules.
n08.e: Mustn't expresses prohibition (the rules forbid it). Don't have to and needn't mean it is not necessary.

n09.e: A wish about an unreal present uses the Past Simple: I wish I had more time. Wish + have is not used.

n09.q: I wish I ____ harder last year.
n09.e: A regret about the past uses the Past Perfect: I wish I had studied harder last year.
Wish + would expresses annoyance about someone's behavior or a change you want: I wish you would stop talking.
It's time + subject takes the Past Simple: It's time we went home, meaning we should go now.

n09.q: He talks as if he ____ everything.
n09.e: As if + past simple expresses an unreal or unlikely comparison: He talks as if he knew everything (but he doesn't).

n09.q: You can borrow my book ____ you return it tomorrow.
n09.e: Provided that means only if: You can borrow my book provided that you return it tomorrow.

n09.q: ____ you hurry, you will miss the train.
n09.e: Unless means if you don't: Unless you hurry, you will miss the train. Do not use another negative with unless.

n09.q: ____ I known about the problem, I would have helped.
n09.e: Had I known = If I had known. This inverted third conditional is formal: Had I known about the problem, I would have helped.

n09.q: If only I ____ the answer! I can't remember it.
n09.e: If only + Past Simple expresses a wish about the present: If only I knew the answer! It means I don't know it.

n09.q: I'd rather you ____ smoke in here.
n09.e: I'd rather + subject + Past Simple expresses a preference about someone else's action: I'd rather you didn't smoke here.

n09.q: Take a jacket ____ it gets cold.
n09.e: In case means because it may happen: Take a jacket in case it gets cold. Unless and provided do not give this meaning.

n09.q: Hurry up, ____ you'll miss the bus.
n09.e: Otherwise means if not: Hurry up, otherwise you'll miss the bus. Although and unless do not fit the meaning.

n10.e: A modal passive uses modal + be + V3: The form must be signed before Friday.
Happen is an intransitive verb (it has no object), so it has no passive: The accident happened last night.
Have + object + V3 is the causative: I had my hair cut means someone else cut it.

n10.q: It is said that he is rich. = He ____ rich.
n10.e: The reporting passive is subject + is said to + V1: He is said to be rich.
A perfect modal passive uses should have been + V3: The window should have been repaired.

n10.q: She is going to ____ her house painted.
n10.e: Have + object + V3 is the causative, and going to is followed by a base verb: She is going to have her house painted.
English receives the action, so use the passive: English is spoken in many countries.

n10.q: I was ____ a book for my birthday.
n10.e: With two objects, either can become the subject: I was given a book. The verb needs V3.
Rice receives the action and the agent is introduced with by, so use the passive: Rice is grown by farmers.

n10.q: The thief ____ by the police last night.
n10.e: The thief receives the action, and the time (last night) is finished, so use the Past Simple passive: was arrested.

n10.q: I need to get my laptop ____.
n10.e: Get + object + V3 is the causative: get my laptop repaired (someone repairs it for me).

n10.q: It is believed that he left the country. = He is believed ____ the country.
n10.e: A past action in the reporting passive uses to have + V3: He is believed to have left the country.

n11.q: Please ____ the light. It's too bright.
n11.e: Turn off the light means to switch it off. Turn up increases volume or brightness; turn on switches on.
Take off means to leave the ground when a plane begins its flight.

n11.q: I'm looking ____ my keys. Have you seen them?
n11.e: Look for means to search for something. Look at means to direct your eyes; look after means to take care of.

n11.q: We have ____ paper. Please buy some.
n11.e: Run out of means to have none left: We have run out of paper.

n11.q: The match was ____ because of rain.
n11.e: Call off means to cancel: The match was called off because of rain.

n11.q: She ____ the offer because the salary was low.
n11.e: Turn down means to refuse: She turned down the offer.
With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun must go between the verb and the particle: Turn it off. Turn off it is wrong.
Look forward to is followed by -ing because to is a preposition here: I look forward to meeting you.
Bring up means to raise a child: She was brought up by her grandmother.
Give up means to stop trying: Don't give up! You can do it.

n11.q: I can't ____ the noise from the street.
n11.e: Put up with means to tolerate: I can't put up with the noise from the street.

n11.q: We ____ the meeting until next week.
n11.e: Put off means to postpone: We put off the meeting until next week.

n12.q: He stopped ____ because it was bad for his health.
n12.e: Stop + -ing means to end an action: He stopped smoking. Stop + to means to pause in order to do something.

n12.q: Remember ____ the door when you leave.
n12.e: Remember + to + V1 means not to forget to do something: Remember to lock the door.
Remember + -ing means to recall a past event: I remember meeting him last year.
Suggest is followed by -ing: She suggested going to the park.

n12.q: The teacher made us ____ the text again.
n12.e: Make + object + base verb (no to): The teacher made us read the text again.
Tell + object + to + V1: He told me to be quiet.
Need + -ing has a passive meaning (it needs to be washed): The car needs washing.

n12.q: She is old enough ____ the exam.
n12.e: Adjective + enough + to + V1: She is old enough to take the exam.

n12.q: I saw him ____ the road. (whole action)
n12.e: See + object + base verb describes a whole action that you saw from start to finish: I saw him cross the road.

n12.q: I tried ____ the window, but it was stuck.
n12.e: Try + to + V1 means to attempt something difficult: I tried to open the window, but it was stuck.
Look forward to is followed by -ing because to is a preposition here: I'm looking forward to seeing you.
Enjoy is followed by -ing, not to + V1: She enjoys reading novels.

n13.q: ____ is a book on the desk.
n13.e: There + be introduces something that exists or is present: There is a book on the desk. Their, those and these cannot do this.
Many students is plural, so use There are: There are many students in the class.
English needs a subject, so use the dummy subject it for weather: It is raining today.
The negative imperative is Don't + base verb: Don't talk. Not talk and Don't to talk are wrong.

n13.q: There ____ a pen and two books on the table.
n13.e: When there is a list, the verb agrees with the first noun: a pen, so there is.
Let's + base verb makes a suggestion: Let's start the lesson. Let alone cannot take a base verb like this.
Have got means the same as have for possession: I have got a new phone.
Emphatic do + base verb adds emphasis: She does like music! Does is used for the third person.

n13.q: ____ a lot of noise in the street last night.
n13.e: There was a lot of noise in the street last night. Noise is uncountable and singular, so there was is correct.
It is used as the subject for weather and temperature: It is hot in Cambodia in April.
The imperative uses the base verb without a subject: Lend me your pen, please.
In a negative sentence, use any with plural and uncountable nouns: There isn't any milk.

n14.e: Child has an irregular plural: children. Childs, childrens and childes are not English words.

n14.q: The ____ books are on the desk. (more than one student)
n14.e: A plural noun ending in -s takes only an apostrophe to show possession: the students' books.
Mathematics ends in -s but is a singular subject name, so it takes a singular verb: Mathematics is difficult.

n14.q: The police ____ looking for the thief.
n14.e: Police is always plural, so it takes a plural verb: The police are looking for the thief.

n14.q: We have a ____ break at eleven.
n14.e: In a compound adjective before a noun, the unit is singular: a ten-minute break. Plurals are used only after the noun (The break is ten minutes).
Children is an irregular plural that does not end in -s, so the possessive is children's.

n14.q: Tom and Mary live together. ____ house is near the school.
n14.e: For joint possession, put 's after the last name only: Tom and Mary's house.
Information is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb: The information is very useful.
Tooth has an irregular plural: teeth. Tooths, toothes and teeths are not English words.
Scissors is a plural noun (it names a tool with two blades), so it takes a plural verb: Scissors are on the table.
A singular noun shows possession with 's: my sister's car. Sisters' would mean more than one sister.

n14.q: We have a ____ holiday next week.
n14.e: Time before a noun is a compound adjective with a singular unit: a two-week holiday.

n15.e: Money is uncountable, so use much: How much money? Many is used only with countable nouns.

n15.q: There are ____ students in the class today than yesterday.
n15.e: Students is countable, so use fewer. Less is used with uncountable nouns (less water).

n15.q: I have ____ friends in this city, so I feel lonely.
n15.e: Few means hardly any, which fits the sad meaning (I feel lonely). A few would mean some.

n15.q: She has ____ time to finish the report, so she is relaxed.
n15.e: A little means some, which fits the positive meaning (she is relaxed). Time is uncountable, so few and many do not fit.

n15.q: Each of the students ____ a book.
n15.e: Each takes a singular verb, even in each of the students: Each of the students has a book.

n15.q: ____ answer is correct. They are both wrong. (two answers)
n15.e: Neither means not one and not the other: it fits because both answers are wrong. Both would mean that both are correct.

n15.q: One pen is red; ____ is blue.
n15.e: The other means the second of two: One pen is red; the other is blue.

n15.q: Some students like tea; ____ prefer coffee.
n15.e: Others means some more of a group (not all): Some students like tea; others prefer coffee.
Some is used in offers and requests, even though the sentence is a question: Would you like some tea?
Any is used with negatives: I don't have any time. Some is used in positive sentences.
With a negative and an uncountable noun (milk), use much: There isn't much milk left.

n15.q: Would you like ____ cup of tea?
n15.e: Another means one more (singular): Would you like another cup of tea?

n16.q: I am ____ in this lesson. It is not interesting.
n16.e: -ed adjectives describe how someone feels: I am bored. -ing adjectives describe what causes the feeling (the lesson is boring).
-ing adjectives describe what causes a feeling: The news was surprising. -ed would describe a person (She was surprised).
The order is opinion before material: a beautiful silk scarf. The other options are in the wrong order or ungrammatical.
The order is age before material: an old wooden house.
A frequency adverb goes before the main verb: She never arrives late.
A frequency adverb goes after the verb be: He is always late.
Do not place an adverb between the verb and its direct object: She speaks English fluently.

n16.q: The lesson was ____ difficult that nobody finished.
n16.e: So + adjective + that describes a result: The lesson was so difficult that nobody finished.
Number comes before opinion: two lovely children. Lovely two children is not the usual order.

n16.q: She has ____ been to Siem Reap.
n16.e: A frequency adverb goes after the first auxiliary verb: She has never been to Siem Reap. Ever is not used in positive statements.

n16.q: It was ____ a long journey that we were exhausted.
n16.e: Such + a + adjective + noun: such a long journey. So is used with an adjective alone (so long).

n16.q: She was ____ by the long speech.
n16.e: -ed adjectives describe how a person feels: She was bored by the long speech.

n17.q: This book is ____ than that one.
n17.e: Interesting has three syllables, so use more: more interesting. Interestinger is not used.
Use the + superlative: the tallest in the class. After the superlative, use in for groups.

n17.q: This test is ____ than the last one.
n17.e: Use much or a lot before a comparative. Very cannot be used before a comparative form.

n17.q: The ____ you practise, the better you become.
n17.e: The + comparative …, the + comparative … shows two connected changes: The more you practise, the better you become.
Not as … as compares equality in a negative way: He is not as tall as his brother.

n17.q: It's the best film I ____ seen.
n17.e: A superlative with ever uses the Present Perfect: It's the best film I have ever seen.
Comparative and comparative shows continuing change: The weather is getting worse and worse.

n17.q: This bag is ____ expensive as that one.
n17.e: Twice as + adjective + as compares multiples: This bag is twice as expensive as that one.

n17.q: This is the ____ hotel in the city.
n17.e: The hotel is compared with all others in the city, so use the superlative: the most expensive.
Neat is one syllable, so use -er for the comparative: neater. More neatest is not correct.

n17.q: He is as ____ as his father.
n17.e: As + adjective + as uses the base form of the adjective: as tall as his father.
A comparative adverb with than: faster than I do. Fast has the same form as an adjective, so the comparative is faster.

n18.e: In a negative sentence use any-: I don't know anything. Nothing would make a double negative.
Everyone is singular, so it takes is: Everyone is ready.
Each other is used when two or more people do the same thing to each other: They help each other.
When the subject and object are the same person, use a reflexive pronoun: She hurt herself.

n18.q: Between you and ____, I think he is wrong.
n18.e: After a preposition use the object pronoun: between you and me. Between you and I is a common mistake.

n18.q: I live ____. I don't share the house.
n18.e: By + reflexive pronoun means alone: I live by myself.
One replaces a singular noun (book) to avoid repetition: I like the red one.
Do not use a reflexive pronoun after feel: I feel tired, not I feel myself tired.

n18.q: I didn't see ____ at the party.
n18.e: After a negative verb use anyone, not no one: I didn't see anyone at the party.
Herself emphasizes that she made the cake alone. Her and she cannot be used for emphasis here.

n18.q: I forgot my pen. Can I borrow ____?
n18.e: Yours is a possessive pronoun that replaces your pen: Can I borrow yours?
Everyone is singular but is often followed by their in modern English: Everyone should bring their own book.

n19.e: Life in general takes no article: Life is hard sometimes.
Jobs take a or an. Teacher starts with a consonant sound, so use a.
Sports take no article: He plays football.
Most single countries take no article: Cambodia. The is used with names like the United States.

n19.q: I'd like to be ____ honest person.
n19.e: Honest begins with a vowel sound (the h is silent), so use an: an honest person.

n19.q: He goes to ____ school by bike. (He is a student.)
n19.e: When school is used for its main purpose (studying), no article is needed: He goes to school.

n19.q: She saw a dog. ____ dog was big.
n19.e: Dog was mentioned before, so use the on the second mention.

n19.q: He is ____ best student in the class.
n19.e: A superlative takes the: He is the best student in the class.
Names with a union or states take the: the United States.

n19.q: ____ Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean.
n19.e: The Pacific Ocean is a specific named ocean, so use the: The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean.
Meals take no article: I have breakfast at seven.

n20.e: Interested is followed by in: She is interested in music.
Good is followed by at: He is good at maths.
Wait is followed by for: They are waiting for the bus.
Discuss is followed directly by its object, so no preposition is used: We discussed the problem.

n20.q: I arrived ____ Phnom Penh at noon.
n20.e: Arrive in is used for cities and countries: I arrived in Phnom Penh. Arrive at is used for small places.
Onto shows movement to a surface: The cat jumped onto the table.
Married is followed by to: She is married to a doctor.
Opposite means facing the school across the street: The bank is opposite the school.
Belong is followed by to: The book belongs to me.
Afraid is followed by of: He is afraid of dogs.
On is used for floors of a building: She lives on the third floor.

n20.q: The train goes ____ a long tunnel.
n20.e: Through shows movement from one side to the other inside something: The train goes through a long tunnel.

n21.q: The girl ____ father is a doctor lives next door.
n21.e: Whose + noun shows possession: the girl whose father is a doctor.

n21.q: My sister, ____ lives in Kampot, is a nurse.
n21.e: Who is used for people in a non-defining clause with commas: My sister, who lives in Kampot, is a nurse.
That is used after everything, all and nothing: Everything that she said was true.

n21.q: The man ____ lives next door is kind.
n21.e: Who is the subject of lives, so it cannot be left out and no extra pronoun is added.

n21.q: The book ____ I bought is useful. Which word can be left out?
n21.e: That is the object of bought, so it can be left out in a defining clause: The book I bought is useful.

n21.q: He passed the exam, ____ surprised everyone.
n21.e: Which can refer to a whole clause: He passed the exam, which surprised everyone.

n21.q: The man ____ there is my teacher. (reduced clause)
n21.e: A reduced relative clause uses the -ing form: The man standing there = The man who is standing there.

n21.q: This is the school ____ I studied.
n21.e: Where = in which and is used for places: This is the school where I studied.

n21.q: The woman to ____ I spoke was kind.
n21.e: After a preposition in formal English, use whom for people: The woman to whom I spoke.

n21.q: The reason ____ he left is unclear.
n21.e: Why is used after the noun reason: The reason why he left is unclear.

n21.q: The teacher ____ I met yesterday is very kind.
n21.e: Who is used for people: The teacher who I met yesterday is very kind.

n21.q: The house ____ roof is red is mine.
n21.e: Whose + noun shows possession: The house whose roof is red is mine.

n22.e: An -ing participle clause describes an action at the same time as the main action: Walking home, I met my teacher.

n22.q: ____ the exam, she left the room.
n22.e: An earlier completed action is shown with having + V3: Having finished the exam, she left the room.
The negative participle clause is Not + -ing: Not knowing the answer, he stayed silent.

o: Walking down the street, the rain started.
Walked down the street, it rained.
Walk down the street, rain started.
Walking down the street, I felt rain.
n22.e: The subject of the participle clause must be the same as the subject of the main clause. Only I can walk down the street and feel rain.

n22.q: ____ in 1990, the book is still popular.
n22.e: A passive participle clause uses V3: Written in 1990, the book is still popular (the book was written).

n22.q: ____ tired, she went to bed early.
n22.e: Feeling tired gives the reason, and the subject (she) is the same in both clauses.
After the conjunction before, use the -ing form: Before leaving, check the lights.

n22.q: Which sentence has a dangling participle?
o: Walking home, I saw my friend.
n22.e: The rain was not walking home, so the participle clause does not match the subject. This is a dangling participle.

n22.q: ____ the road, he saw a snake.
n22.e: Crossing the road describes the same subject at the same time: Crossing the road, he saw a snake.

n22.q: ____ by the teacher, the student felt proud.
n22.e: A passive meaning needs V3: Praised by the teacher, the student felt proud.

n22.q: ____ the door, she turned on the light.
n22.e: An action done just before another uses -ing: Opening the door, she turned on the light.

o: Having finish his homework, he watched TV.
Finished his homework, he watched TV.
Having been finish his homework, he watched TV.
Having finished his homework, he watched TV.
n22.e: Having + V3 shows that the first action finished before the second: Having finished his homework, he watched TV.

n23.e: After when, use a present tense for the future: I'll call you when I arrive.

n23.q: ____ I was sleeping, the phone rang.
n23.e: While is followed by a clause: While I was sleeping. During is followed by a noun.
During is followed by a noun (the storm): We stayed inside during the storm.
Since + a point in time with the Present Perfect: I have lived here since 2020.

n23.q: By the time I arrived, they ____.
n23.e: The leaving happened before the arrival, so use the Past Perfect: By the time I arrived, they had left.

n23.q: By the time you arrive, I ____.
n23.e: By the time + present gives a Future Perfect in the main clause: By the time you arrive, I will have left.

n23.q: Finish the report ____ Friday. (not later than)
n23.e: By means not later than a deadline: Finish the report by Friday. Until means continuing up to a time.
Until means up to the time that: Wait here until I come back.
Until means up to the time that: I'll wait until you finish. By expresses a deadline, not continuing.

n23.q: She has worked here ____ five years.
n23.e: For + a length of time with the Present Perfect: She has worked here for five years.

n23.q: Please call me as soon as you ____.
n23.e: After as soon as, use a present tense for the future: Please call me as soon as you arrive.
During is followed by a noun phrase (the film): He fell asleep during the film.

n24.q: It was ____ a hot day that we stayed inside.
n24.e: Such + a + adjective + noun + that: It was such a hot day that we stayed inside.

n24.q: It was ____ hot that we stayed inside.
n24.e: So + adjective + that: It was so hot that we stayed inside. Such is used before a noun.
Too + adjective + to + V1 means more than is needed: He is too tired to study.

n24.q: She is ____ to vote, so she can register.
n24.e: Adjective + enough + to + V1: She is old enough to vote.
Although is followed by a clause: Although it rained, we went out.
Despite is followed by a noun: Despite the rain, we went out.

n24.q: I study ____ I can pass the exam.
n24.e: So that + can/could/will/would introduces a purpose: I study so that I can pass the exam.

n24.q: There were ____ many students that we had no space.
n24.e: So many + noun + that shows a result: There were so many students that we had no space.
However begins a new sentence with a comma and shows contrast: It rained. However, we went out.

n24.q: We don't have ____ time to finish.
n24.e: Enough comes before a noun: We don't have enough time to finish.

n24.q: The box was ____ heavy for me to lift.
n24.e: Too + adjective + to + V1: The box was too heavy for me to lift.

n24.q: She studied hard ____ she could pass the exam.
n24.e: So that + clause expresses purpose: She studied hard so that she could pass the exam.

n25.e: After a negative adverb such as never, the auxiliary comes before the subject: Never have I seen such a beautiful view.

n25.q: Not only ____ sing, but she also danced.
n25.e: Not only + did + subject + base verb: Not only did she sing, but she also danced.

n25.q: Hardly ____ arrived when it began to rain.
n25.e: Hardly had + subject + V3 + when: Hardly had we arrived when it began to rain.

n25.q: ____ I known, I would have helped.
n25.e: Had I known = If I had known: Had I known, I would have helped.

n25.q: It was Sophea ____ won the prize.
n25.e: It was Sophea who won the prize. In an it-cleft, who is used for people.
In a wh-cleft, the wh-clause is the subject and is the verb: What I need is a rest.
After rarely, use inversion with do/does/did: Rarely does he arrive late.

n25.q: No sooner had she arrived ____ it started to rain.
n25.e: No sooner had + subject + V3 + than: No sooner had she arrived than it started to rain.

n25.q: Little ____ he know that she was waiting.
n25.e: Little + did + subject + base verb: Little did he know that she was waiting.

n25.q: Under no circumstances ____ open this door.
n25.e: After under no circumstances, use inversion: Under no circumstances should you open this door.

n25.q: It was in 2019 ____ I moved to Phnom Penh.
n25.e: In an it-cleft, that introduces the focused time: It was in 2019 that I moved to Phnom Penh.

n25.q: Only after the exam ____ I feel relaxed.
n25.e: After only after, use inversion with did: Only after the exam did I feel relaxed.

n26.e: A positive statement is agreed with so + auxiliary + subject: So do I.
A negative statement is agreed with neither + auxiliary + subject: Neither can I.
A short answer repeats the auxiliary of the question: Yes, I do.
Hardly is already negative, so do not add don't: I hardly know him.

n26.q: She didn't say ____ about the problem.
n26.e: Use anything after a negative verb: She didn't say anything about the problem. Nothing would make a double negative.
I hope not means I hope it will not rain. No and don't cannot be used here.
The statement is Past Simple, so the agreement uses did: So did I.
The statement is Present Perfect, so the agreement uses have: So have I.
The statement uses am, so the agreement uses am: So am I. So do I would be used after other verbs.
The statement is negative with have, so the agreement uses neither + have: Neither have I.
I think so replaces a whole clause (he will come): Will he come? I think so.

n26.q: She ____ eats meat. She is almost a vegetarian.
n26.e: Hardly ever is already negative: She hardly ever eats meat. Do not use another negative with it.

n27.e: An indirect question uses statement word order (subject + verb): where the bank is.
An indirect question has no do/does/did: what time it starts.

n27.q: Do you know ____ he is coming?
n27.e: A yes/no question becomes an indirect question with if or whether: Do you know if he is coming?
A reported question uses statement order and backshift: where I lived.
The question word is the subject, so no do is used: Who called you?
The question word is the object, so did is used: Who did you call?

n27.q: “What is she like?” asks about her ____.
n27.e: What is she like? asks for a description of her personality or appearance. How is she? asks about her health.

n27.q: How ____ is it from here to the market?
n27.e: How far asks about distance: How far is it from here to the market?

n27.q: I'd like to know ____ she lives.
n27.e: After I'd like to know, the question word is followed by statement order: where she lives.

n27.q: Can you tell me ____ the library opens?
n27.e: After Can you tell me, use statement order with no do: when the library opens.

n27.q: He asked me ____ I wanted tea or coffee.
n27.e: Whether introduces a choice in an indirect question: He asked me whether I wanted tea or coffee.

n27.q: ____ pen is this? It belongs to Dara.
n27.e: Whose asks about possession: Whose pen is this? It belongs to Dara.

n28.e: A reported question uses statement order and backshift: She asked me where I lived.

n28.q: He told ____ that he was late.
n28.e: Tell is followed by an object, with no to: He told me that he was late.
Suggest is followed by -ing: She suggested going home early.

n28.q: He asked if I ____ come to the party.
n28.e: Will changes to would after backshift: He asked if I would come to the party.

n28.q: “Study hard,” said the teacher. → The teacher told us ____ hard.
n28.e: Tell + object + to + V1 is used for reported commands: The teacher told us to study hard.

n28.q: He said that water ____ at 100°C. (general truth)
n28.e: A general truth does not need backshift: He said that water boils at 100°C.
Promise + to + V1: She promised to call me.
Accuse is followed by of + -ing: He accused me of cheating.

n28.q: “I must go,” she said. → She said she ____ go.
n28.e: Must changes to had to in reported speech for obligation: She said she had to go.
Apologize is followed by for + -ing: She apologized for being late.

n28.q: She said, “I am tired.” → She said that she ____ tired.
n28.e: After backshift, am changes to was: She said that she was tired.

n28.q: He asked me, “Do you speak Khmer?” → He asked me ____ I spoke Khmer.
n28.e: A yes/no question is reported with if: He asked me if I spoke Khmer.

o: Because it rained, we stayed home.
n29.e: A complete sentence needs a main clause. Because it rained, we stayed home has one: we stayed home. Because it rained alone is a fragment.

n29.q: Which sentence has a comma splice?
o: I was tired, so I went to bed.
I was tired, I went to bed.
I was tired; I went to bed.
I was tired. I went to bed.
n29.e: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma. Fix it with a conjunction, a semicolon or a full stop.

n29.q: Choose the sentence with parallel structure.
o: She likes swimming, to run and cycling.
She likes to swim, running and cycling.
She likes swimming, running and cycling.
She likes swim, running and to cycle.
n29.e: The items in a list must have the same form: swimming, running and cycling are all -ing forms.

o: He studied hard, so he passed.
n29.e: A run-on sentence joins two clauses with no punctuation or conjunction: He studied hard he passed.
A sentence needs one subject, so My teacher he is kind has a double subject. The correct form is My teacher is kind.

o: He is both smart and works hard.
He is both smart and hardworking.
He is both smartly and hardworking.
He is both smart and to work hard.
n29.e: With both … and, the two parts must have the same form: both smart and hardworking (both adjectives).

n29.q: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
o: Walking home, I felt the rain.
n29.e: The rain cannot walk home, so the opening phrase does not match the subject. This is a dangling modifier.

o: She was tired, but she worked.
Tired as she was, she worked.
n29.e: Although she was tired is a dependent clause and cannot stand alone. It needs a main clause.

o: She is tired, so she is going home.
She is tired so, she is going home.
She is tired she is going home.
She is tired, she is going home.
n29.e: A comma and a conjunction (so) should join the two clauses: She is tired, so she is going home.

o: He likes to read, writing and to draw.
He likes to read, to write and to draw.
He likes reading, to write and drawing.
He likes read, writing and drawing.
n29.e: With three items in a list, they must all have the same structure: to read, to write and to draw.

n29.q: Choose the best way to fix “The weather was bad we stayed home.”
o: The weather was bad, we stayed home.
The weather was bad so, we stayed home.
The weather was bad, so we stayed home.
The weather was bad we stayed, home.
n29.e: A conjunction with a comma fixes the run-on: The weather was bad, so we stayed home.

o: The students who finished the test.
n29.e: A complete sentence has a subject and a main verb: The students finished the test. The other options are fragments.
